lead: A Turing machine is the simplest machine that reads, writes and moves on an unlimited tape. A finite control holds one state, a head scans one cell, and the tape supplies as much memory as the run needs. This chapter gives the formal definition, shows moves as tables and diagrams, and explains the instantaneous description — the snapshot of tape, state and head that records a run.
prereq: You need Unit 1 on alphabets, strings and finite automata: a Turing machine's finite control is a DFA that can also write on a tape.

blocks.text: A Turing machine has three parts. The finite control holds exactly one state from a finite set Q. The head scans one cell. The tape is a row of cells holding symbols from a finite alphabet Γ; it is unbounded to the right, and every cell past the input holds the blank symbol □.

The tape is the memory. A finite automaton cannot count because it has nowhere to store a count. A Turing machine writes a mark, walks away, and reads it later. That one change takes it from regular languages to everything computable.

Formally a Turing machine is a 7-tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q<sub>0</sub>, q<sub>accept</sub>, q<sub>reject</sub>). Q is the finite set of states. Σ is the input alphabet; the input string is written on the tape before the run. Γ is the tape alphabet, the symbols that may appear on the tape. δ is the transition function. q<sub>0</sub> ∈ Q is the start state. q<sub>accept</sub> and q<sub>reject</sub> are halting states, with q<sub>accept</sub> ≠ q<sub>reject</sub>.
The alphabets are linked: Σ ⊆ Γ, and the blank □ is in Γ but not in Σ, so □ ∉ Σ. An input string never contains a blank; blanks fill unwritten cells.
One move is decided by two things only: the current state and the symbol under the head. The transition function has the type
δ : Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}
blocks.where: Q is the set of states, Γ the tape alphabet, L and R the head directions left and right. The input pair is (state, symbol read); the output triple is (new state, symbol written, direction).

blocks.text: The symbol written replaces the symbol read, so writing the same symbol leaves the tape unchanged. δ is a partial function: it need not be defined for every pair. If δ(q, a) is undefined, the machine halts in state q. That is an ordinary stop, separate from q<sub>accept</sub> and q<sub>reject</sub>.

A transition table has states as rows and tape symbols as columns. A filled cell holds the triple, for example "q<sub>1</sub>, 1, R"; an empty cell means δ is undefined there. A transition diagram draws one circle per state and one arrow per defined entry, labelled "a → b, R": in state q, reading a, write b, move right, go to p. Entries with the same destination and direction share one arrow.
This machine is deterministic: at most one move is possible in any situation. Section 5.4 adds choices and extra tapes.
A snapshot of the tape, the state and the head position is the instantaneous description (ID); some syllabi call it a configuration.

Write the tape as one string and cut it at the head. The ID is α q β. Here α is the cells strictly left of the head, q is the current state, and β is the cells from the scanned cell rightwards, so the first symbol of β is under the head. Blanks right of the head are never written; a head on a blank cell gives β = □. Blanks left of the head stay in α, because they record how far right the head has gone: tape 1 with the head on cell 2 is 1□q, not 1q. If the head is on the leftmost cell, α is empty and the ID starts with q.
α<sub>1</sub> a q b β<sub>1</sub> ⊢ α<sub>1</sub> p a c β<sub>1</sub>
blocks.where: when δ(q, b) = (p, c, L). The head scans b and a is the cell to its left; a, b, c are tape symbols; α<sub>1</sub>, β<sub>1</sub> are strings; q, p are states. Write c over b, move left, and p now sits just before a.

blocks.text: α<sub>1</sub> q b β<sub>1</sub> ⊢ α<sub>1</sub> c p β<sub>1</sub>
blocks.where: when δ(q, b) = (p, c, R). Write c over b, move right, so p sits just after the written symbol.

blocks.text: These rules define the yield relation ⊢. Its reflexive transitive closure ⊢* means zero or more moves. A halting configuration has no next ID: the state is q<sub>accept</sub> or q<sub>reject</sub>, or δ is undefined for the scanned pair. A run is a chain C<sub>0</sub> ⊢ C<sub>1</sub> ⊢ … ⊢ C<sub>k</sub> of IDs ending in a halting configuration; k is the number of moves.

figure.caption: The finite control holds the single state, the head reads and writes one cell, and blanks fill every cell past the input.

spec.title: Turing machine parts
spec.aria: A finite control controls a read/write head that scans one cell of a tape; blank cells extend to the right.

examples.question: A Turing machine M has Q = {q<sub>0</sub>, q<sub>1</sub>, q<sub>2</sub>, q<sub>accept</sub>, q<sub>reject</sub>}, Γ = {0, 1, □}, Σ = {0, 1}, and δ(q<sub>0</sub>, 0) = (q<sub>1</sub>, 1, R), δ(q<sub>1</sub>, 0) = (q<sub>2</sub>, 0, R), δ(q<sub>2</sub>, □) = (q<sub>accept</sub>, □, L); all other entries are undefined. The input is the string 00. Write the sequence of instantaneous descriptions from the start to the halting configuration and state the number of moves.
steps: Start: cells 0 and 1 hold 0 and 0, the rest are blank, the head is on cell 0, the state is q<sub>0</sub>. α is empty and β = 00, so the ID is q<sub>0</sub>00.
Apply δ(q<sub>0</sub>, 0) = (q<sub>1</sub>, 1, R): write 1 on cell 0, move right to cell 1, state becomes q<sub>1</sub>. Tape is 10, so the ID is 1q<sub>1</sub>0.

Apply δ(q<sub>1</sub>, 0) = (q<sub>2</sub>, 0, R): write 0 on cell 1 (no change), move right to cell 2, state becomes q<sub>2</sub>. Cell 2 is blank and the head is on it, so β = □ and the ID is 10q<sub>2</sub>□.
Apply δ(q<sub>2</sub>, □) = (q<sub>accept</sub>, □, L): write □, move left to cell 1, state becomes q<sub>accept</sub>. Tape is still 10, so the ID is 1q<sub>accept</sub>0.
That ID halts, because q<sub>accept</sub> is a halting state. Count the moves: three transitions were applied.
examples.answer: The run is q<sub>0</sub>00 ⊢ 1q<sub>1</sub>0 ⊢ 10q<sub>2</sub>□ ⊢ 1q<sub>accept</sub>0, and the machine halts after 3 moves.

traps: In α q β the state sits immediately before the scanned symbol. Writing q<sub>0</sub>00 as 00q<sub>0</sub> puts the head after the input, a different ID.
Never drop the scanned cell, even when it is blank: a head on a blank cell gives β = □. Never pad β with blanks to the right.
Σ and Γ are not the same set. The blank is in Γ but never in Σ, so an input string never contains □.
δ undefined means the machine halts; it does not mean accept. Acceptance needs the state qaccept, as Section 5.2 explains.
The triple is ordered (new state, symbol written, direction). Writing happens in the scanned cell before the head moves.

The tape is unbounded only to the right. If δ(q, a) = (p, b, L) and the head is on the leftmost cell, the move is illegal: treat δ on that pair as undefined. A correct design never asks for such a move.

quiz.q: Give the type of the transition function of a deterministic single-tape Turing machine and name the three parts of its output.
quiz.a: δ : Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}. The output triple is the new state, the symbol written on the scanned cell, and the head direction L or R.

quiz.q: State the relation between Σ, Γ and the blank symbol □ in the formal definition.
quiz.a: Σ ⊆ Γ. The blank □ is in Γ but not in Σ, so □ ∉ Σ and no input string contains a blank.

quiz.q: Why is δ allowed to be a partial function, and what does an undefined entry mean for the run?
quiz.a: δ need not give a move for every (state, symbol) pair. If δ(q, a) is undefined, the machine stops in state q with no next ID; this is a halting configuration, though not necessarily an accepting one.

quiz.q: In an ID α q β, what does each part stand for, and which blanks are written?
quiz.a: α is the tape content strictly left of the head, q is the current state, and β starts at the scanned cell and runs rightwards. Blanks right of the head are dropped, so a head on a blank cell gives β = □. Blanks left of the head stay in α.

quiz.q: A machine has δ(q<sub>0</sub>, 1) = (q<sub>1</sub>, 0, R) and δ(q<sub>1</sub>, 1) = (q<sub>accept</sub>, 1, R), with all other entries undefined. On input 11, write the ID sequence and give the number of moves.
quiz.a: Start ID q<sub>0</sub>11. After the first move: 0q<sub>1</sub>1. In state q<sub>1</sub> reading 1, write 1 and move right to blank cell 2: the ID is 01q<sub>accept</sub>□. It halts, so the number of moves is 2.

quiz.q: The ID is 10q<sub>2</sub>□ and δ(q<sub>2</sub>, □) = (q<sub>accept</sub>, □, L). Write the resulting ID.
quiz.a: The head scans blank cell 2, and a = 0 is the cell to its left. Write □, move left, state becomes q<sub>accept</sub>: the new ID is 1q<sub>accept</sub>0, and the run halts.

quiz.q: A student writes the start ID of the input 00 as 00q<sub>0</sub>. Explain the error and describe the tape situation this written ID actually represents.
quiz.a: In α q β the state is placed just before the scanned symbol, so the start ID is q<sub>0</sub>00: α empty, head on the first 0. The string 00q<sub>0</sub> would mean the head is on the cell after the two input symbols, a blank cell, with the whole input to the left of the head — a different ID.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real machines have finite memory, so the unbounded tape models "enough tape". Busy-beaver search programs implement these definitions literally, and a machine that visits more distinct IDs than it has configurations can never halt. Undo stacks in editors are practical cousins of the yield relation.
